prompt: A dynamic array (C# List<T>, JS Array) doubles its capacity when full. What is the amortized cost of Add/push?
explanation: Each resize copies n elements, but resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ... so the total copy work over n appends is < 2n. Spread over n operations that is O(1) amortized, even though a single append can cost O(n).

prompt: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from n unsorted elements using bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last internal node to the root)?
explanation: Most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a short distance. Summing n/2^(h+1) nodes × h work over all heights h gives a convergent series, so the total is O(n). Inserting elements one by one would be O(n log n).

prompt: Solve the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n log n).
explanation: Each of the log n levels of the recursion tree does about n·log(n/2^i) work. Summing log n + log n − 1 + ... gives Θ(log² n) per n, so Θ(n log² n). Plain Master theorem case 2 doesn't apply directly; the extended case 2 (k = 1) gives n log^(k+1) n.

prompt: In a hash table using separate chaining, what is the worst-case lookup time if every key hashes to the same bucket?
explanation: All keys land in one chain, so lookup degrades to a linear scan. This is why hash-flooding attacks exist, and why runtimes like .NET randomize string hashing and Java converts long chains into balanced trees (O(log n)).

prompt: In C#, a class used as a Dictionary key overrides Equals() but not GetHashCode(). What is the most likely outcome?
options: A compile error, because the two must be overridden together
Lookups by a logically equal (but different) instance usually fail
Everything works, since Dictionary only calls Equals()
Lookups always succeed but get slower
explanation: Dictionary first picks a bucket using GetHashCode(). The default is reference-based, so two equal-by-value instances land in different buckets and Equals() is never consulted. The compiler only warns (CS0659). Records and value tuples generate both correctly.

prompt: Given an integer array that may contain negatives, how do you check in O(n) whether any contiguous subarray sums to k?
options: Sort the array, then binary search
Keep running prefix sums in a hash set and check whether (prefix − k) was seen before
It can't be done faster than O(n²) when negatives are allowed
explanation: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i−1], so you need some earlier prefix equal to prefix[j] − k. Seed the set with 0. A sliding window only works when all numbers are non-negative, because the window sum then changes monotonically.

prompt: What does an in-order traversal of a binary search tree produce?
explanation: In-order visits left subtree, node, then right subtree. The BST invariant (left < node < right) makes that ascending order, which is also how you validate a BST in O(n).

prompt: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm return wrong answers on some graphs?
options: It fails on graphs with cycles
It fails when edge weights are negative
It fails when two paths have equal length
explanation: Dijkstra finalizes a node when it is popped, assuming no later path can be shorter. A negative edge can break that assumption. Use Bellman-Ford (O(VE)), which also detects negative cycles.

prompt: Which method reliably detects a cycle in a directed graph (for example, circular dependencies between services)?
options: BFS, flagging any node seen twice
DFS that tracks nodes on the current recursion stack (gray/black coloring), or Kahn's algorithm leaving nodes unprocessed
explanation: A directed cycle exists exactly when DFS finds a back edge to a node still on the stack (gray). Kahn's topological sort detects the same thing when it can't consume every node. Union-Find and "seen twice" only work for undirected graphs: a diamond A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D reaches D twice with no cycle.

prompt: Which two properties make a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?
options: Greedy choice property and a sorted input
Divide and conquer with independent subproblems
explanation: Optimal substructure means you can build the optimal answer from optimal sub-answers. Overlapping subproblems means the same sub-answers recur, so memoizing them pays off. Merge sort has the first property but not the second.

prompt: What is the time complexity of the classic DP for minimum-coin change with n coin denominations and target amount A?
explanation: dp[a] = min over coins c of dp[a − c] + 1. That is A states × n transitions, using O(A) space. This is pseudo-polynomial: it is polynomial in the value of A, not in the number of bits needed to write A.

prompt: What is the best-known time complexity for finding the length of the longest increasing subsequence?
explanation: Keep tails[k] = the smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each element, binary-search tails and replace (or append). tails stays sorted, so each step is O(log n). The simple DP is O(n²).
